# Remote-desktop endpoint config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/remote-desktop-endpoints/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.RemoteDesktopEndpointBlock` (ADR-085 D1) declaring one device the `remote-desktop` environment provider may be pointed at. The block label is the endpoint name.

**This directory is the whole reachable estate.** An environment recipe names an endpoint — `config { endpoint = "bench-pi" }` — and can express no host, no port and no credential: `pkg/config.EnvironmentConfigBlock` declares no such attribute, so a recipe that tries fails to parse. That is the ADR-057 D7 confused-deputy guard one level out, and it holds harder here: a `host:port` an agent can pass is a port scan, and the substrate is the operator's physical estate. PRD-013 §9.2 (amended) states the consequence plainly — for an attached substrate there is nothing local to contain, so the network reach to the device *is* the boundary. There is no Seatbelt or Landlock behind this file.

**Declaring an endpoint is not granting one.** Reachability is a separate RBAC resource under the ADR-060 one-model rule: `remote-desktop/endpoints/<name>/attach`, granted from an ordinary `role` recipe and evaluated by the ordinary ACL engine, with the ordinary `+` / `#` wildcards. Deny-by-default — a declared endpoint that no role grants is reachable by nobody, and **holding the tool is not authorization to reach a device**. No standard role grants this family; `admin` reaches it only through its existing `#`.

The two refusals — an *undeclared* endpoint and a *declared* endpoint the principal lacks the grant for — are distinct code paths, both fail closed, and neither reports the endpoint's existence differently from its absence: same message, same shape, same timing class. An inventory an unauthorized caller can enumerate by probing names has given away the estate, so the refusal is deliberately unhelpful to the caller and fully detailed in the operator's log.

`transport` is a field rather than part of the provider type (ADR-085 D0/D3): v1 implements `rfb` only and unset means `rfb`, but the seam exists from the first commit so a future RDP transport is an implementation behind the same verbs rather than a second provider. `credential` must be a reference (`env://`, `keychain://`, `vault://`) and never a literal, for the same reason `llm_account.credential` must be — a literal would commit the device's password to the vault, where `tera config pull` exports it.

`username` is that rule's mirror image and the two are easy to confuse. An account name is an *identity*, not a secret, so it is written literally and a reference is refused — an operator reaching for symmetry would otherwise present the string `env://…` to the device as an account name and read the far side's rejection as a wrong password. It is also the field that decides **which credential the attach presents**: naming an account selects RFB security type 30 (Apple Diffie-Hellman — what a stock macOS Screen Sharing server offers, authenticating a real account with a full-length password) in preference to the legacy type 2 (no username, 8 bytes of DES) on a target offering both. Naming none preserves the earlier preference exactly. A username with no `credential` is refused rather than ignored, since type 30 authenticates an account *and* a password. The type and the account both appear on the provider's attach log line; the credential reference appears on neither. Against a target offering *no* type that carries a username — an ordinary VNC server, say — the attach still succeeds on the password alone, and the account it could not present is reported as a WARN rather than left to be inferred from a green endpoint.

`max_attaches` bounds how many concurrent Tera-managed attachments this one device will carry, across every principal (ADR-093 D5). Optional, and **unset means unlimited** — which is what every declaration written before the field existed already means, so adding it broke nothing and requires no migration. It is not the same knob as `admission { desktops { count = N } }`: that one is per-*principal* across every endpoint, this one is per-*endpoint* across every principal, and each refusal says which it is. It is a **contention control, not a security control** — the count is of attachments this daemon made, so a person at the console and any other viewer are outside it, unobservable and un-evictable, and `max_attaches = 1` does not make an endpoint exclusive. The security boundary is the grant above. A non-positive value is refused at authoring time: `0` is a withdrawal written in the wrong field, and the way to close an endpoint is to delete the declaration or the grant.

Status: **preview**.

## Example

A minimal `remote-desktop-endpoints`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/remote-desktop-endpoints/example-remote-desktop-endpoint.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

remote_desktop_endpoint "example-remote-desktop-endpoint" {
  address = "127.0.0.1:5900"
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | block label | Endpoint name — the only identity a recipe or an agent ever handles. A bare identifier: letters, digits, hyphen and underscore, starting with a letter or digit. An address-shaped name is rejected. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | Human-readable description of which device this is. Worth writing, and read by two audiences: a grant on this endpoint may hand an agent a physical machine, and this string is what a reviewer decides that on — and, since ADR-093 D8, what a granted MCP caller reads in the desktop tool's own per-caller endpoint listing. Carried verbatim, so write it for both. |
| `address` | string | yes | — | — | — | host:port of the device. Required. Never reaches an agent — this field is the reason the endpoint set is operator-declared (ADR-085 D1). |
| `transport` | string | no | — | — | — | Wire protocol. v1 supports rfb only; unset means rfb. A field rather than part of the provider type, so a second transport is not a second provider (ADR-085 D0/D3). |
| `username` | string | no | — | — | — | Account name to authenticate as, for a security type whose authentication has one — RFB type 30 (Apple Diffie-Hellman), which a stock macOS Screen Sharing server offers. A plain string, not a credential reference: a username is an identity, not a secret, and it is logged beside the endpoint name at attach. Declaring it makes the client prefer type 30 over the legacy type 2 on a target offering both; leaving it unset preserves the previous preference. Requires credential. At most 63 bytes, no NUL. |
| `credential` | string | no | — | — | — | Credential reference (env://, keychain://, vault://) for the device's authentication. Optional — RFB's None security type is real. Never a literal: tera config pull would export it. |
| `max_attaches` | integer | no | — | — | — | Ceiling on concurrent Tera-managed attachments to this one device. Optional — unset means unlimited. Must be at least 1. Per-endpoint across every principal, unlike admission { desktops { count } }, which is per-principal across every endpoint. A contention control, not a security control: it counts only attachments this daemon made, so a person at the console or any other viewer is outside it and cannot be evicted (ADR-093 D5). |
